name: Umar Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Umar. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. To start, could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hearthside, a care co-op, so the carers own a share of it, which is why the pay's better than the agencies. Most of my shifts are evenings and overnight sits with people who have dementia, in their own homes. A typical night I get to Mrs Farouk's at eight, help her with her tea and tablets, get her settled, then I'm up maybe three times when she wanders or gets confused about where she is. I'm still learning, to be honest, I'm slower than the others at handling the bad nights calmly. The quiet hours at three in the morning, that's what wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside of work, what's your life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my mate Kofi, who's a plumber. I did four years in a parcel warehouse before this, lived cheap, and saved most of it, so I've got a good few months put by, more like a year really. I use the AI chat thing now and then, mostly to tidy up my spelling on the care notes, because I left school early and I'm not great with writing. I vote at every co-op meeting and I always vote for whoever backs public services and unions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to Kofi, who's been saying robots will fix boilers for years. At the co-op I'd say good, now let's talk about pay and staffing instead. Online I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd be a relief, but nothing much changes for me. Night sits are about being there, and no program does that. The money's fine, I've savings, and there are jobs everywhere for carers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my shifts and keep thinking about the nursing associate apprenticeship the local hospital runs. I'd keep using the AI thing for my spelling, because it saves me ten minutes a night. And I'd keep going to the co-op members' meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit bored at the idea, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the apprenticeship. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Confidence, mostly. I failed English at school and the course has essays. I can sit with a frightened woman at three in the morning, but a two-page essay makes me sweat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your night look like five years from now in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same, maybe with a better phone for the notes. Mrs Farouk might not be with us by then, sadly. There'll be someone else who needs a calm person in the night.

say: I'd tell Kofi I told you so and push the co-op to talk about **pay and staffing**.
I'd say little online, since I rarely **post** anything.
think: Night sits are about **being there**, and no program can do that.
My **savings** and plenty of local jobs mean nothing much changes for me.
do: Carry on with my **overnight sits** at Hearthside.
Keep weighing the **nursing associate** apprenticeship at the local hospital.
Keep using AI to fix my **spelling** on care notes.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by the idea.
S0.quote: I can sit with a frightened woman at three in the morning, but a two-page essay makes me sweat.
fieldNote: His savings from **warehouse work** give him real freedom at twenty-seven.
His main block on progress is **confidence** with writing, not money.
He uses AI in a small, **practical** way that suits a steady adopter.

steps.text: Keep doing three overnight dementia sits a week for Hearthside
Keep using the AI chat tool to tidy spelling in care notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the co-op should decide how the AI is used, not some software company. If it's doing the rota and the notes, fine, but the members vote on it. I'd say that loudly at the meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think it's mostly good for me. The bit I'm worst at is the writing, and if the AI does the handover notes from what I say into the phone, that's my weak spot gone. The robots spreading slowly doesn't scare me much yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for whatever training the co-op runs on the new system, once a couple of the others have tried it. And I'd finally apply for the nursing associate apprenticeship, because if the writing's easier, my main excuse is gone. I'd keep my savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, maybe a bit excited. There's a little worry about the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which office staff do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joy and Petra do the scheduling and the family phone calls. They're members like me, so if the AI does their job, it's our problem as a co-op. A co-op that sacks its own office staff because a computer is cheaper isn't really a co-op anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try it first. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been burned before. The co-op tried an app two years ago that lost half our notes. I'm not going first, but I'll be second or third.

say: I'd say the **co-op members** should vote on how AI is used.
I'd insist the decision is ours, not a **software company**'s.
think: AI writing handover notes would remove my **weak spot**, so it's mostly **good** for me.
Robots spreading slowly doesn't **scare** me yet.
do: Take the co-op's **training** on the new system once others have tried it.
Apply for the **nursing associate** apprenticeship this year.
feel: **Calm** and a bit excited, with some worry for the **office staff**.
S1.quote: A co-op that sacks its own office staff because a computer is cheaper isn't really a co-op anymore.
fieldNote: He sees AI as **removing a barrier**, his writing, rather than a threat.
His worry is for **co-op colleagues** in the office, framed as a values test.
He is a classic **second adopter** after a bad app experience.

steps.text: Join the co-op's training on the new notes system after early users
Apply for the hospital's nursing associate apprenticeship this year
Argue at the members' meeting that office staff keep their jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong public rules and why workers have to own a slice of the machines. I'd probably post that, for once. I'd say the co-op model is the answer, if carers own the robots, the money stays with us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, two years for AGI and robots by 2031 is fast. The night sits might last a bit longer than daytime care, because robots doing dementia at three in the morning sounds hard, but I wouldn't bet on it. If I'm a nursing associate by then, I'm also in the firing line from the thinking AI, so I don't know which way to jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still start the apprenticeship, because nursing has more hands-on and judgement than care notes. I'd push the co-op to look at buying robots ourselves instead of losing work to a big firm. I'd keep my savings, maybe put a bit into the co-op as a member loan if they needed it. And I'd use the AI more, to understand what it can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, honestly. Like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is to blame if it goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies and the government for letting them run it. They'll sell robots to the big care chains first, and those chains already pay badly. Workers won't get a say unless they've organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mrs Farouk's son, who visits on Sundays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm still here and I'll be here as long as I can. I'd tell my client Mrs Farouk's son that a robot can watch his mum all night, but it won't know which song calms her down. That's true, at least for now.

say: I'd call for **public rules** and for workers to own a slice of the machines.
I'd say the **co-op model** keeps robot money with carers.
think: Robots by **2031** might reach night sits later, but I wouldn't bet on it.
Nursing could also be hit by **thinking AI**, so I'm unsure which way to jump.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** anyway, since nursing mixes hands-on work and judgement.
Push Hearthside to **buy robots** itself rather than lose work to big firms.
Use **AI tools** more to learn their limits.
S2.quote: I'd tell my client Mrs Farouk's son that a robot can watch his mum all night, but it won't know which song calms her down.
fieldNote: He turns the threat into a **co-op ownership** question, which fits his politics.
His career move to **nursing** feels less certain once thinking AI is fast.
His savings give him **control**, so he is worried but not alarmed.

steps.text: Start the nursing associate apprenticeship in the next intake
Propose at Hearthside that the co-op buys its own care robots
Use the AI chat tool weekly to see what it can do
Lend some savings to the co-op as a member loan if asked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to get the rules right, so let's not waste them. At the co-op I'd ask for a plan, with dates. Online I'd share stuff from the care workers' union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the one where I can actually finish my training and have a few years of using it. Thinking AI by 2031, robots by 2034, so if I qualify by 2029 I get some years in before it bites. But I'd be thirty-five by 2034 and still might need another change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next year and stick with it. I'd push the co-op to make a five-year plan, including which robots we'd buy and who'd look after them. I'd keep saving and maybe start using the AI every day to get the hang of it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, but more hopeful than the fast one. It feels like a race I could actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might still need another change. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe being the person who looks after the robots on a patch, checks what they've done, talks to the families. Somebody still has to ring a daughter and tell her that her dad had a bad night, and I'd want that somebody to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and the gym, easy. Kofi and I would maybe look at a cheaper flat. I'm not touching the savings unless I'm out of work.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to get the rules right and shouldn't waste them.
I'd ask the co-op for a **dated plan** and share union posts.
think: This timeline lets me **qualify** by 2029 and work some years before robots in **2034**.
I might still need **another change** at thirty-five.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** next year and stick with it.
Push the co-op for a **five-year plan** on robots and staff.
Use **AI daily** to learn it properly.
feel: **Worried** but more **hopeful**, like a race I could run.
S3.quote: Somebody still has to ring a daughter and tell her that her dad had a bad night, and I'd want that somebody to be me.
fieldNote: He imagines a future role **supervising robots** and talking to families.
Five years makes his training feel **worth finishing**.
He still expects his **care income** could shrink by his mid-thirties.

steps.text: Start the nursing associate apprenticeship next year
Ask Hearthside members to vote on a five-year robot plan
Use AI tools every day to plan nights and write notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time if we organise now. I'd tell people at the co-op that we could be the ones running the robots in our town by 2039. I'd sound fairly upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a whole career for me. I'd qualify, get experience, maybe move up, and by 2039 I'd be thirty-seven with real skills. The night sits would change, but I'd have time to change with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the apprenticeship, then maybe the full nursing degree after, paid by the hospital. I'd keep putting money aside, maybe into a flat with Kofi or on my own. And I'd stay active at the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a bit uneasy about the people who won't move in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older carers at Hearthside. Brenda's been doing this for thirty years and hates her phone. Ten years is plenty for someone my age, but my colleague Brenda will be sixty-five by then and nobody will retrain her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd buy somewhere sooner, since I'd know my income for a while. Kofi talks about buying together. I'd want a deposit saved by thirty.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty if we **organise now**.
I'd tell the co-op we could be **running the robots** in our town.

By **2039** I'd be thirty-seven with real skills.

Save a **deposit** for a flat by thirty.
feel: Fairly **calm**, uneasy about **older colleagues** who won't move in time.

fieldNote: His worry shifts from himself to **older colleagues** like Brenda.
Ten years turns his plan into a **full career** path.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship and apply for a hospital-funded nursing degree
Save a flat deposit by age thirty
Keep voting and speaking at Hearthside members' meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't know which way to jump. Nursing might be hit by the thinking AI and care by the robots. What would help is the co-op having money to buy its own robots, and the government paying for training, not just leaving it to the market.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the nights. People think care is days. The worst hour in care is three in the morning, when a confused old woman thinks you're a burglar and you have to stay gentle.

headlineQuote: The worst hour in care is three in the morning, when a confused old woman thinks you're a burglar and you have to stay gentle.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** night carer at a worker-owned **co-op**, still learning to handle bad nights calmly.
Four years of warehouse saving give him about a **year's cushion** and real freedom.
He uses AI to fix his **spelling** and sees it as removing his weak spot.
He is calm in the slow pictures and **anxious** in the AGI ones, unsure whether nursing is safe.
His answer is always **collective**: carers owning the robots through the co-op.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nursing and care could both be hit before he knows which way to jump.
whatWouldHelp: Money for the **co-op** to buy its own robots.
**Government-paid training** instead of leaving it to the market.
